AARON ALDERMAN / SOURCERER

Make the magic answerable.

On building things people can understand, question and change.

A personal essay · A working reflection, open to correction

I like the moment an idea becomes something you can use: a description turns into a page, a question becomes an experiment, a small tool removes a difficulty. There is wonder in that transition. I want the wonder to survive a closer look.

Sourcerer is the name for this side of my work. It brings curiosity about the world together with the craft of making systems. The question beneath both is what would let another person understand the work well enough to question it, use it responsibly and change it.

IN THIS ESSAY

  1. Start with the distinction that matters.
  2. Make meaning something people can work with.
  3. Ask who is allowed to make the change.
  4. Let a check say exactly what it established.
  5. Design for the moment something goes wrong.
  6. Leave people with capability they can keep.

01

Start with the distinction that matters.

Before building an answer, I need to be clear about the question. What did we observe? What are we trying to make possible? Which part of the explanation is supplied by evidence, and which part have I chosen?

A model is useful partly because it leaves things out. I want those omissions to remain visible beside its results. A neat diagram, a persuasive story or a familiar mathematical form can help me think without establishing that the world behaves that way.

The same discipline matters in software. A screen may look complete while the meanings beneath it are still vague. Naming the people, objects, decisions and relationships gives us something more specific to inspect than an attractive interface.

02

Make meaning something people can work with.

The process algebra is a way of describing actions and how they compose: what an action receives, what it changes, which conditions it requires and what follows. It lets a definition do practical work instead of remaining a comment beside unrelated code.

That does not remove the need for judgment. Someone still chooses what a term means and whether the definition is suitable. I want those choices to have names, sources and versions, so another person can ask what has been assumed and what an edit would alter.

The aim is a closer relationship between what we say a system does and what it actually executes. When that relationship is incomplete, the missing connection should be visible. A declaration on its own is not a deployed capability.

03

Ask who is allowed to make the change.

Being able to run an operation does not settle whether I am entitled to run it. A proposed change needs a person or role with the relevant authority, a clear scope and a chance to inspect what will happen.

AI assistance makes this distinction especially useful. A suggestion can help someone understand a matter without gaining permission to act for them. Producing fluent text, finding a plausible plan and authorising its consequences are different steps.

A refusal can be a useful result. A system that says the source changed, the authority is absent or the proposal exceeds its scope is giving us information we can act on. I would rather preserve that boundary than make apparent success depend on silently crossing it.

04

Let a check say exactly what it established.

A passing test should have a readable scope. It may show that a calculation reproduces, that a document preserves its structure or that a request was checked against a particular rule. Those are useful achievements. Their names should match their reach.

Reproducing a result does not make its assumptions true. An internally consistent account can still describe the wrong situation. A prototype can demonstrate an operation while leaving reliability, accessibility or real-world usefulness unresolved.

I want adverse results to remain part of the record. A counterexample, a failed comparison or a missing source can save more work than another convincing demonstration. The explanation should remain able to change when the evidence does.

05

Design for the moment something goes wrong.

Change needs memory. I want to be able to ask which definition was active, what someone proposed, who accepted it and what the system actually did. A useful history preserves differences instead of compressing them into a story in which everything was always intended.

Replay and undo also need honest meanings. Replaying a recorded sequence can reproduce the sequence without reproducing a person’s reasons. Reversing a local edit does not necessarily reverse an email already sent, a disclosure already made or someone else’s lost time.

The engineering question is therefore specific: what can be reversed, what needs a new decision, and what requires repair outside the software? I want that question in the design before the first confident click.

06

Leave people with capability they can keep.

A good tool should make its user more capable of understanding and acting. That asks for readable explanations, useful exports, inspectable definitions and a way to continue when the original maker is absent.

Temple, Sourcery, Worldwright and the other projects explore parts of that ambition. Their individual maturity still matters. The wider purpose does not let me describe an intended connection as a completed service.

The magic I want to make is something a person can live with: useful enough to matter, legible enough to question and bounded enough that helping does not quietly become taking over.

A question before the next build

What does this operation mean, who may authorise it, what evidence supports it, and what happens if it is wrong?
